## Approach

**Forced conflicts.** Nodes 0, 1, 5, 10, 16 form a 5-clique, so at least one must be spilled. Node 1 is precolored and cannot be spilled. Nodes 0, 5, 16 are each adjacent to a precolored node of color 1 or 2, which leaves them only colors {0, 3} between them, so they cannot all stay. Spilling 16 (cost 4) resolves this and breaks the 5-clique.

**Propagating the coloring.** With 16 spilled, I colored greedily with backtracking. Two more blockages appeared:
- Node 12 is adjacent to 0, 1, 8, and 11. Those already cover all four colors, so 12 is spilled (cost 1).
- Node 15 forces the chain that makes node 26 unavailable, so 15 is spilled (cost 2) instead of 26 (cost 4).

**Final blockages.** After those spills, node 21 has neighbors using all four colors, so it is spilled (cost 7). Node 27 is then blocked for the same reason, so it is spilled (cost 1).

**Result.** Spilled set {12, 15, 16, 21, 27} with total cost 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 1 = 15. I checked every edge among the 23 remaining nodes, and each has differently colored endpoints. The precolored nodes keep their colors (8 and 24 at color 1, 1 at color 2).

I did not prove this is globally optimal. I found it by a guided search with backtracking, so a cheaper spill set may exist.
